title: PS-2 Effects of protein supplementation to backgrounding cattle in a winter bale grazing system on growth performance, forage production and soil health
content:
Abstract
To evaluate how supplemental protein source (PS; dried distiller’s grains plus solubles (DDGS) or soybean meal (SBM)) and frequency (SF; daily or 3 times weekly) of winter bale-grazing backgrounding cattle on growth performance, forage production and soil health. Seventy-two crossbred calves (BW = 249 ± 27 kg) grazed for a 44-d period. Calves were blocked by sex, stratified by BW, and randomly assigned to treatments. Each paddock contained 10 grass hay bales (495 ± 32.6 kg) and was 0.18 ha. Calves were supplemented on a dry matter basis with daily receiving 0.75% of BW and three times a week receiving 1.75% of BW. Blood and BW were collected on d 0, 28, and 44. Plasma was analyzed for non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA) and plasma urea nitrogen (PUN). Dry matter intake (DMI) was estimated by weighing residue from one bale per paddock. Forage biomass was estimated by clipping 0.25 m2 frames and soil samples (0-0.15 m and 0.15-0.3 m) were collected 0, 1.5, 3, and 4.6 m from bale center from three bales in each paddock. Soil samples were analyzed for total carbon (TC), total nitrogen (TN), Olson phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and organic matter (OM). Data was analyzed using the MIXED procedure in SAS. There were no PS × SF interactions (P ≥ 0.49) for ending body weight (EBW), average daily gain (ADG), dry matter intake (DMI) or biomass. There were no differences (P ≥ 0.32) due to SF for EBW, ADG or DMI. There were no differences (P = 0.21) due to PS for EBW and ADG. Estimated DMI tended (P = 0.09) to be greater for cattle supplemented with SBM than DDGS. Plasma urea nitrogen was influenced (P < 0.05) by PS, SF, day, and all interactions. The data suggests increased PUN with increased CP. NEFA tended (P = 0.09) to be influenced by SF and the interaction of SF × day (P = 0.08). Forage biomass was influenced (P = 0.0002) by distance from bale center but did not differ (P=0.91) between treatments. Paddocks supplemented three times weekly had lower (P < 0.05) TC across depths. Total N (0-0.15m) tended (P = 0.053) to increase in SBM fed paddocks. K was greater (P = 0.008) toward the bale center. There was a tendency (P ≥ 0.053) for increased soil OM (0.15-0.3m), TN (0-0.15m) and TC (0-0.15m) for SBM fed daily paddocks. The results suggest that SBM supplementation improved soil health and producers can utilize an extended winter bale grazing system with backgrounding cattle while supplementing either DDGS or SBM as few as three times a week with minimal influences on animal performance. The decision to replace DDGS with SBM should be based on cost and availability.
